text.supports: Tatami sizes: kyoma 1.91x0.955 m, chukyoma 1.82x0.91, edoma 1.76x0.88; reached commoners' homes toward the end of the 17th c.
Ken = 6 shaku = 1.82 m; ~1.97 m under Hideyoshi; reduced to 1.818 m c.1650
Kyoma: ken 6.5 shaku, tatami 6.3 x 3.15 shaku, tatami-based planning vs Edo column-based (inakama); term attested 1608
Plot 5.4-6 m wide x ~20 m deep; mushiko-mado; 1, 1.5 or 2 storeys; bengara koshi
Low tsushi-nikai (regulated), board/kokera roofs early, 1720 (Kyoho 5) tile + dozo encouragement, udatsu, facade elements, Kyoto vs Edo (dashigeta) differences
Sangawara = pan and roll combined in one tile
Sangawara invented 1674 by Nishimura Hanbei (Miidera); lighter than hongawara; commoner tile roofs first restricted, later encouraged
Udatsu: machiya gable parapet; Edo-period fireproof tiled and plastered form, status symbol
Mushiko-mado: plastered slatted window lighting the low upper storey (zushi)
Hongawara: flat pans + semicylindrical covers; special eave, ridge, verge tiles
Kido gates at both ends of each cho in Edo/Kyoto/Osaka; guard hut 6 x 9 shaku, eave 10 shaku; closed about 10 pm, wicket door after
Jobikeshi towers from 1658, 3 jo (~9 m), plain wood; daimyo and town towers black and lower; Kyoho: one tower per ~10 cho, ladders on jishinban
Fire-tower history (corroborates T12)
Kyoto Odoi 1591: 22.5 km, base ~20 m, top ~5 m, height ~5 m, moat 10-15 m, bamboo on top, 10 gates, opened up in the Edo period
Hakone checkpoint c.1619-1869: two gates ~18 m apart, guard houses, palisades, lookout; 'iri-deppo ni de-onna'; 1686 staffing
Castle-town zoning (samurai, chonin, temple districts); walls mostly only around the castle, some sogamae; masugata gates, cranked streets
Doma earth floor, hiroma raised ~50 cm, roof types, irori, status markers (ridge members, udatsu)
Post-station facilities: honjin, waki-honjin, hatago, kichin-yado, chaya, toiyaba, kosatsu
Honjin reserved features: front gate, shikidai genkan, jodan-no-ma; system from 1634-35
Tokaido 100 porters + 100 horses per station (1638); Kiso/Nakasendo 50 + 50
Toiyaba = relay office for horses/porters; surviving examples Fuchu, Narai, Samegai
Ichirizuka ordered 1604; paired mounds ~5 ken square, 1 jo high, every ri (~3.9 km); trees: enoki 55 %, pine 27 %, cedar 8 %
Kosatsu boards at kosatsuba (Nihonbashi, Sanjo bridge...); 1711 Shotoku boards stayed up to the end of Edo
Mitsuke: guarded gates (Edo castle's 36 mitsuke) and guard posts on roads
Sugidama at sake breweries from the early Edo period; green when new, browns with age
Magariya: L-plan farmhouse with stable, 18th c., Nanbu (Iwate)
First Edo bathhouse 1591; zakuro-guchi; upper-floor rest room for men; 1791 mixed-bathing ban
Jinya: single-compound administrative seat (office, residence, storehouses, walls, gate); Takayama Jinya
Nagaya-mon: plaster walls allowed for samurai residences, boards for commoners
Hatago: two-storey, lattice fronts, 200-300 mon/night, ~3,000 on the Tokaido
Edo north/south machi-bugyo; ~250 staff for 500,000 townspeople
Stone lantern parts and types (kasuga, yukimi, ikekomi, oki)
Torii parts; shinmei vs myojin families; vermilion pillars, black only on kasagi/nemaki; stone torii since the 12th c.
Nozura-zumi, uchikomi-hagi, kirikomi-hagi; less stone walling in east Japan
Dosojin at village edges, passes, crossroads; most surviving are Edo/Meiji; Nagano densest
Commoner stone grave markers spread in the Edo period (danka system); family graves from mid-Meiji
Multi-chamber climbing kiln standard in the Edo period
Waterwheels widespread in the Edo period for rice polishing/milling
Uchinori (door-head) height traditionally 5 shaku 7 sun (~1.73 m); 8 shaku (2.42 m) ceilings
Stone-weighted board roofs ~3.5 sun (~20 deg); late 17th c. sangawara displaced board roofs in Edo
Ordinary thatched minka mostly <= 45 deg; gassho near 60 deg (read via search summary)
Sun-kobai: rise in sun per 1 shaku run; 3 sun ~17 deg
Zushi-nikai: street-side upper storey 1.5-1.8 m high; storage/servants; mushiko windows
Why the Edo-period zushi-nikai ceiling was low (question record)
Zushi-nikai design notes (Kyoto machiya)
Post sizes: 3.5 sun (10.5 cm) and 4 sun (12 cm) standard
Daikokubashira: larger central post on the toriniwa side
1668 (Kanbun 8) Edo townsmen house rules: no nageshi, sugito, tsuke-shoin, carving, karakami; 3-ken beam-span limit
1683 ban on gold thread, embroidery, so-kanoko for townspeople; 1745 townspeople limited to silk, tsumugi, cotton, hemp; 'shijuhacha hyakunezumi'
Women's obi ~25 cm in the 1730s; men's widest ~16 cm in the 1730s; tied at the back by the end of the 17th c.
Kosode: small sleeve openings, sleeves sewn to the body, rounded outer edges
Dictionary hex values for traditional colour names (used only where no photo sample)
Hakone road paved with stone in 1680, 2 ken (~3.6 m) wide, kerb stones 30-70 cm (read via search summary)
Daihachiguruma handcart after the 1657 fire; bed 8 x 2.5 shaku, wheels 3.5 shaku; 1,273 in Edo in 1703
Coloured nishikigoi arose in Niigata in the early 19th c. (so: none in a 1730 world)
Nagaya form: shared walls, own entrance, kitchen at the door, 1-2 rooms
Honjin for daimyo/officials only; waki-honjin could take others
Tatami reached ordinary commoners' homes by the late Edo period
E. S. Morse, 'Japanese Homes and Their Surroundings': drawings of ridges, gables, kura, inns (images c26-c28)
